mean: understanding a plan or situation in the same way
ex: Before the client call, let's make sure the whole Hyderabad team is on the same page about pricing.
with: get everyone on the same page
note: Fine at work; very common in meetings, a little cliché in formal writing. It means shared understanding, not always full agreement.

mean: to say or do something that helps strangers relax and start talking
ex: At hostel orientation, Rohan tried to break the ice by asking everyone which home food they missed most.
note: Casual and fine at work. An 'icebreaker' is a game or question used for this at workshops.

mean: in trouble, usually because of something you did
ex: Kabir landed in hot water with the principal after posting the exam timetable as a meme.
note: Casual; fine in spoken work talk. Used for trouble you caused yourself, not plain bad luck.

mean: very rarely
ex: My brother in Toronto calls once in a blue moon, usually when he needs a document from home.
with: only once in a blue moon
happen once in a blue moon
visit once in a blue moon
note: Casual. Hindi says a rarely seen person has become 'ईद का चाँद'; in English you would say 'We hardly ever see you!'

mean: to learn how to do something after some practice
ex: Riding a scooter in Guwahati traffic is scary at first, but you'll get the hang of it in a week.
note: Casual but fine at work. Followed by 'it' or a noun or -ing word: 'get the hang of cooking'.

mean: the most important fact, or the final result
ex: We can debate the design all day, but the bottom line is that the app must launch before Diwali.
note: Fine at work; overused in speeches. In business it also means profit, so 'hurt the bottom line' = cut profit.

mean: not able to decide between two choices or sides
ex: Ritu is still on the fence about taking science or commerce after Class 10.
note: Fine at work. 'Sitting on the fence' can sound critical: avoiding a choice to stay safe. Use 'about' + topic.

mean: an idea that is worth thinking about carefully
ex: The retired judge's talk on fairness gave the law students plenty of food for thought.
note: Fine at work and in writing, but a cliché as an essay ending. No 'a': say 'food for thought', not 'a food for thought'.

mean: a situation where the rules are unclear, neither clearly right nor wrong
ex: Whether delivery riders count as employees is still a grey area in labour law.
note: Fine at work and in formal writing. British spelling 'grey'; American 'gray area'.

mean: a small, visible part of a much bigger problem
ex: The ten fake degree cases caught this year may be just the tip of the iceberg, officials warned.
with: just the tip of the iceberg
only the tip of the iceberg
merely the tip of the iceberg
instead: a small part of a bigger problem
note: Fine at work and in news, but a cliché; use it once. Almost always about problems, rarely good things.

mean: back at the start, because the first attempt failed
ex: The landlord backed out at the last minute, so we're back to square one in our flat hunt in Koramangala.
note: Casual; fine at work. It means the effort so far was wasted and you must start over.

mean: to do something cheaply or quickly by skipping important steps
ex: Engineers say the flyover cracked because the contractor chose to cut corners on cement and steel.
note: Fine at work; always critical. Use 'cut corners on' + what was skimped. Not the same as a clever shortcut or jugaad.

mean: a big, obvious problem that everyone avoids talking about
ex: At the family meeting about Dadi's house, the loan Chacha never repaid was the elephant in the room.
with: address the elephant in the room
ignore the elephant in the room
the elephant in the room is
note: Fine at work, a little overused. 'Let's address the elephant in the room' is a polite way to raise an awkward issue.

mean: something that has both good and bad effects
ex: Working from home is a double-edged sword: no Gurugram traffic, but the workday never seems to end.
note: Fine at work and in writing; Hindi uses the same picture. A cliché in essays, so don't lean on it.

mean: someone who argues the other side on purpose to test an idea
ex: Let me play devil's advocate: what if customers in small towns don't want home delivery at all?
note: Fine at work. Usually 'play devil's advocate'. You may not believe the view yourself; you are testing the plan.

mean: to unfairly change the rules or targets after someone has started
ex: Every time we meet the sales target, the regional head seems to move the goalposts again.
note: Fine at work, but it is a complaint about unfairness. From football. Often 'keep moving the goalposts'.

mean: to finally do something hard or unpleasant that you have been avoiding
ex: After months of back pain, Sunita decided to bite the bullet and book the surgery.
note: Casual; fine at work. Used for accepting a hard choice, not for bravery in danger.

mean: something that seemed bad at first but turned out to be good
ex: Missing the flight to Goa was a blessing in disguise; that evening I met my future business partner.
with: turn out to be a blessing in disguise
instead: bad luck that turned out well
note: Casual and fine at work; a cliché in essays. Said afterwards, once the good side shows. Hindi: 'जो होता है, अच्छे के लिए होता है'.

mean: to understand a hidden meaning that is not said openly
ex: The HR email only says 'restructuring', but read between the lines and you can see layoffs coming.
with: learn to read between the lines
if you read between the lines
note: Fine at work. Careful: you can also 'read in' meanings that were never there.

mean: an unimportant point that pulls attention away from the real issue
ex: In the meeting on hostel fees, the dress-code question was a red herring that ate up half an hour.
note: Fine at work and in formal writing; common in mystery stories and debates. It misleads, often on purpose.

mean: the biggest part of something
ex: Bengaluru and Delhi still take the lion's share of startup funding in India.
note: Fine at work and in writing. It means the largest part, not all of it, and often hints the split is unfair.

mean: a trap where you cannot win, because each condition blocks the other
ex: It's a catch-22 for freshers: companies want experience, but you can't get experience without a job.
note: Fine at work and in writing; often written 'Catch-22', after Joseph Heller's 1961 novel. Use it for circular traps, not any hard choice.

mean: to stop trying because you are happy with past success
ex: Topping the district in Class 10 is great, Aditi, but don't rest on your laurels in Class 11.
note: Fine at work and in writing. Change 'your' to fit: our, their, its. Laurels were the leaf crowns given to winners in ancient Greece.

mean: a win that cost so much that it was hardly worth winning
ex: Winning the boundary case after twelve years and lakhs in fees was a pyrrhic victory for the Shetty brothers.
note: Formal writing and news. Often capitalised 'Pyrrhic', after King Pyrrhus, who beat Rome but lost much of his army. Say PIR-ik.

mean: a so-called choice where you must take the one thing offered or nothing
ex: With only one bus to the village after 6 pm, it was Hobson's choice: squeeze into the 6:10 or walk home.
note: Formal and a bit old-fashioned. Not a hard choice between two options (that is a dilemma); it is no real choice at all.

mean: the idea that the simplest explanation that fits the facts is usually right
ex: The fan stopped and so did the fridge; by Occam's razor, it's a power cut, not two broken machines.
note: Formal and academic. A rule of thumb, not proof. Named after William of Ockham, a 14th-century English friar.
